q: Diffraction is defined as the bending of waves around the corners of an obstacle (or) through an aperture into the region of geometrical shadow of the obstacle (or) aperture.
e: True. It is obvious when the opening is comparable to the wavelength, not when the hole is huge. Intensity does not set the bend; wavelength versus size does. Diffraction is bending around an obstacle or through an aperture into the geometrical shadow.

q: Diffraction is defined as the reflection of waves around the corners of an obstacle (or) through an aperture into the region of geometrical shadow of the obstacle (or) aperture.
e: False. Diffraction is bending around an obstacle or through an aperture into the geometrical shadow, not reflection. Reflection is a bounce. Light in the shadow region is the diffraction clue.

q: The amount of bending depends on the wavelength of light relative to the size of the aperture.
e: True. Monochromatic work uses one lambda so patterns do not smear. Aperture is the circular hole light goes through. f-number is focal length divided by that diameter.

q: The amount of bending depends on the intensity of light relative to the size of the aperture.
e: False. How much the wave bends depends on wavelength relative to the aperture size, not on intensity. Long waves through a small hole spread more. Brightness does not set the diffraction angle.

q: If the aperture is much larger than the wavelength of light, the bending will be almost unnoticeable.
e: True. f-number is focal length divided by that diameter. Small f-number means a wide hole for dim light. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating.

q: If the aperture is much smaller than the wavelength of light, the bending will be almost unnoticeable.
e: False. If the aperture is much larger than the wavelength, bending is almost unnoticeable. If the aperture is comparable to or smaller than lambda, diffraction is obvious. The inequality in this statement is backwards.

q: There are two main classes of diffraction, which are known as Fresnel diffraction and Fraunhofer diffraction.
e: True. Fraunhofer is the infinite-distance, plane-wavefront limit. Those two classes are the split in this chapter. Fraunhofer diffraction treats source and screen as infinitely far, giving plane wavefronts.

q: There are three main classes of diffraction, which are known as Fresnel diffraction, Fraunhofer diffraction and Rayleigh diffraction.
e: False. The two main classes here are Fresnel and Fraunhofer. Rayleigh is a resolution criterion, not a third diffraction class in this listing. Finite versus infinite distance is the split.

q: Fresnel diffraction: The source of light and the screen are at a finite distance from the obstacle causing the diffraction.
e: True. Those two classes are the split in this chapter. Fresnel diffraction keeps source and screen at finite distance from the obstacle, so the wavefront is curved. Fraunhofer is the infinite-distance, plane-wavefront limit.

q: Fresnel diffraction: The source of light and the screen are at an infinite distance from the obstacle causing the diffraction.
e: False. Fresnel diffraction keeps finite distances from the obstacle, so the wavefront is curved. Infinite distance is Fraunhofer. Swap those and the curvature assumption flips.

q: Fraunhofer diffraction: There is an infinite distance between the source and the screen from the obstacle.
e: True. Fraunhofer diffraction treats source and screen as infinitely far, giving plane wavefronts. Lenses often create that condition in the lab. Finite distance is Fresnel work.

q: Fraunhofer diffraction: There is a finite distance between the source and the screen from the obstacle.
e: False. Fraunhofer treats source and screen as infinitely far, giving plane wavefronts. Finite distance is Fresnel. Lab Fraunhofer work uses lenses to mimic that infinity.

q: The diffraction pattern consists of a bright central portion (the central maximum).
e: True. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima. Half-integer path difference is a minimum.

q: The diffraction pattern consists of a dark central portion (the central minimum).
e: False. Single-slit diffraction has a bright central maximum, not a dark central minimum. Dark fringes sit on either side. The centre is the strongest bright band.

q: On either side there are alternating bright and dark fringes.
e: True. It depends on wavelength; red fringes sit farther apart than violet. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. Either side there are alternating bright and cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: On either side there are only bright fringes.
e: False. On either side of the central maximum you get alternating dark and bright fringes, not only bright ones. Intensity of those outer bright fringes falls off. Minima are part of the pattern.

q: Each successive bright fringes becomes less intense proceeding outward, away from the central maximum.
e: True. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. In Young's setup it is lambda D over d. It depends on wavelength; red fringes sit farther apart than violet.

q: Each successive bright fringes becomes more intense proceeding outward, away from the central maximum.
e: False. Successive bright fringes become less intense as you go out from the central maximum. The centre is the strongest. Energy is concentrated in that central band.

q: When they arrive at the screen, they interfere destructively and produces a dark fringe (minimum intensity) called the first minimum.
e: True. Young's dark fringes are the half-integer path-difference case. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. In Young's setup it is lambda D over d.

q: When they arrive at the screen, they interfere constructively and produces a dark fringe (minimum intensity) called the first minimum.
e: False. The first minimum is destructive interference, not constructive. Constructive at that angle would be a bright fringe. Path difference from the slit edges is what cancels there.

q: The width of the central maximum depends on width of the slit.
e: True. Many equal slits make a grating with sharp principal maxima. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima.

q: The width of the central maximum is independent of the width of the slit.
e: False. Central-maximum width is 2 lambda D / a, so it depends on slit width a. Wider slit, narrower central bright band. Independent of a would freeze that width.

q: The narrower slit causes the wider central maximum.
e: True. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima. A single slit spreads light into a wide central maximum of width 2 lambda D / a.

q: The wider slit causes the wider central maximum.
e: False. A wider slit makes a narrower central maximum. The formula has a in the denominator. Narrow the slit if you want that central band to spread.
